title: Agentic AI Implementation Path: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Agent Patterns: ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Reflection, and Tool Loops”, what is the central focus?
options: Lesson 22 built the loop by hand. This lesson gives that loop its names. You learn the four patterns that dominate real agent work: ReAct (reason and act interleaved), plan-and-execute (plan first, then execute), reflection (evaluate and revise), and the tool loop they all run on, plus when each one earns its complexity.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Lesson 22 built the loop by hand. This lesson gives that loop its names. You learn the four patterns that dominate real agent work: ReAct (reason and act interleaved), plan-and-execute (plan first, then execute), reflection (evaluate and revise), and the tool loop they all run on, plus when each one earns its complexity.

questions.question: What is the precise difference, as stated in the lesson, between a dead provider behind an OPEN circuit breaker versus one without it?
options: With a circuit breaker open, the provider is removed from the rate limiter, so quotas are never exhausted
An open circuit makes retries faster by doubling their frequency until the provider recovers
An open circuit means requests are buffered until the cooldown elapses instead of being rejected
A dead provider costs one fast rejection per request instead of one full timeout, which is the difference between a clean failover and a cascading slowdown
questions.explanation: The lesson cites this as the whole value of the open state: requests fail immediately (skip to fallback) without waiting out a full timeout, so a dead provider costs a fast rejection rather than a full timeout per request, separating a clean failover from a cascade.

questions.question: The lesson says a backup can meet the database RPO and still fail the retrieval RPO. What does that mean?
options: The database restore succeeded but the indexes were rebuilt with different ANN parameters
Rows were restored cleanly, but the retrieval system was not restored to a known semantic state, so search returns old chunks or mixes embedding model versions
The physical backup was taken before the last write was committed
The restore ran faster than the recovery time objective allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: you restore the database cleanly, the application comes back, but support search returns old policy chunks and mixes two embedding model versions in the same result set. The backup met the database recovery point but failed the retrieval recovery point.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance on a review board?
options: A review board should approve every AI use so no decision escapes oversight.
A review board should not approve every AI use, should not replace system owners, and should produce decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk.
A review board should be made up only of technologists so technical risk is fully understood.
A review board should replace the people who build, buy, own, and operate each AI system.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives three disciplines that keep a review board from becoming theater: it should not approve every AI use (that creates a bottleneck), it should not replace system owners (a named person stays accountable for each system), and a useful meeting produces decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk. A committee made of a single discipline, and a committee that does the building and owning, are presented as failures.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Frameworks overview - LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK”, what is the central focus?
options: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows. This lesson surveys the five frameworks you will actually meet in the wild, and it is honest about what each one is for. LangChain is an integration ecosystem. LangGraph is a stateful graph runtime for workflows that branch and loop. CrewAI is a role-based layer for teams of agents with jobs and backstories. The OpenAI Agents SDK is a deliberately tiny set of primitives with clean handoffs and guardrails. The Claude Agent SDK gives the agent a computer with built-in file, shell, and edit tools. You will learn the mental model behind each one, see the same small task written in two of them so the difference is concrete, and finish with a decision path for choosing a framework instead of trusting star counts.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
"Agent" is the most abused word in enterprise AI right now.
"Agent" is not the most abused word in enterprise AI right now.
questions.explanation: "Agent" is the most abused word in enterprise AI right now.

questions.question: Per the lesson “RAG Quality: Reranking, Hybrid Search, Metadata Filtering, and Freshness”, what is the central focus?
options: The four levers that turn a RAG demo into a system you can trust: reranking to fix top-k precision, hybrid search so exact terms still win, metadata filtering so access control and scope survive retrieval, and freshness so the answers do not go stale.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The four levers that turn a RAG demo into a system you can trust: reranking to fix top-k precision, hybrid search so exact terms still win, metadata filtering so access control and scope survive retrieval, and freshness so the answers do not go stale.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Incident Response for Agents", what must happen before any rollback, restart, or credential revocation when you confirm an agent incident?
options: Export or snapshot the incident window's trace tree to storage independent of the production system
Delete the affected sessions' logs so the bad behavior is not preserved
Revert to the last known-good prompt immediately to stop the bleeding
Restart the agent to clear its in-memory state before investigating
questions.explanation: The lesson: a rollback swaps the running version and a restart clears in-memory state, and either can overwrite or orphan the exact span-level record the postmortem needs. So you freeze or export the trace first, to storage independent of production, before any recovery action.

questions.question: The lesson says two things must be settled before you scaffold the project. Which pair does it name?
options: The model provider and the hosting region
The prompt wording and the token budget
What the agent may do autonomously versus what requires a human, and what counts as a good run
The software license and the repository visibility
questions.explanation: The lesson says to write down the autonomous-versus-human boundary because it becomes the permissions model, and to define what a good run looks like so the test set is real tickets with known routes rather than a vibe check.

questions.question: What cost discipline does the lesson say keeps an eval quality gate from being switched off?
options: Run the full LLM-as-judge suite on every commit to catch regressions early
Use cheap code-based graders in CI on every commit and reserve expensive LLM-as-judge evaluations for preview and production
Run no automated evals and rely on manual review of a few prompts before each release
Run expensive evals only on Fridays so the bill stays low
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a gate costing real money on every commit gets switched off the first month, so it wires the cheap code-based layers into every-commit CI and reserves the expensive judges for preview and production evaluation.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance: Data Residency, Audit Logging, and Retention for AI Systems”, what is the central focus?
options: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders. Audit logging keeps an immutable record of what happened, per action, so a regulator or an investigator can reconstruct it later. Retention puts a clock on how long you keep any of it. This lesson reads the EU AI Act's record-keeping article and GDPR's storage-limitation principle, then shows how a real agent pipeline turns its own event stream into an auditable trail.

questions.question: How does LoRA make adapting a large model affordable compared with full fine-tuning?
options: It pre-computes all weight updates ahead of time so no gradient calculation happens during training.

It freezes the base model and trains a small set of low-rank update matrices A and B, dropping GPT-3-scale trainable parameters from billions to about 18 million and cutting GPU memory by roughly two thirds.
It shrinks the training dataset by selecting only the highest-loss examples.
It replaces the base model with a much smaller model that requires no training at all.
questions.explanation: LoRA keeps the original weight matrix W frozen and represents the adaptation as the product of two smaller matrices, so the adapted weight becomes W plus B times A. Because those small matrices hold far fewer parameters, trainable parameters collapse, with the IBM reference putting GPT-3 full fine-tuning at about 175 billion versus roughly 18 million under LoRA and GPU memory reduced by about two thirds. The rank r is a tunable hyperparameter where a lower rank means fewer trainable parameters but can cost accuracy.

questions.question: Autonomy is decided per action rather than per agent. In the worked service desk example, what rung does an access grant above the standard role template sit at?
options: L2, because a server access change is reversible
L1, because one wrong package is expensive to unwind
L0: the agent retrieves the policy and prepares the evidence packet, and a human decides
L3, because the ticket history provides a labelled set to measure against
questions.explanation: The worked example puts the access grant above the standard template at L0, read and summarize with no write, while a human makes the decision. L1 belongs to the catalog software installation, and the labelled history is what supports the new-starter path to L2.

questions.question: How does the lesson say a capability eval becomes a regression eval?
options: A capability eval is deleted as soon as it passes so the suite stays small
A capability eval is refreshed from new production output each quarter
A capability eval that hits a persistently high pass rate graduates into the regression suite, where it starts measuring whether the behavior still works reliably
A capability eval is run only by human graders once it passes
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the self-healing structure: once an eval hits a persistently high pass rate it graduates from asking can we do this at all to asking can we still do this reliably, so nothing already proven can quietly regress.

questions.question: Meridian's Triage agent rejects a candidate in March. In June, the candidate asks for an explanation under Colorado's automated decision-making law. The team kept 24-hour trace retention and edits prompts directly in a console with no versioning. What does lesson 80 say the failure is, and what is the fix?
options: No failure, because Colorado's 30-day explanation duty only covers the developer of the tool, not the deployer using it
No failure, because an adverse-action explanation only needs the model's name and the score threshold, both of which are in the policy document

The failure is evidentiary: the 30-day plain-language explanation requires decision-time context (inputs, retrieved documents, model version, prompt version), and 24-hour retention plus unversioned prompts means the team cannot reconstruct what the system actually did in March; keep trace logs long enough to answer within the statutory window and version prompts like code
The failure is legal only, so the team should amend the policy document to state that explanations are available on request and move on
questions.explanation: The lesson names the adverse-action explanation as one of two gaps that show up in almost every version of this exercise. Colorado requires deployers to give a plain-language description of the tool's role within 30 days of an adverse decision. Most agents produce a score and rationale at decision time and then lose the retrieval context, so if trace retention is 24 hours the team cannot answer in week three, let alone month three. The fix is to set retention against the longest statutory window and to version prompts and model changes so the team can say what the system was on the day of the disputed decision.

questions.question: Three weeks after stage 1 opened, the human edit rate on drafted returns has risen from 12 percent to 24 percent. Complaint volume and customer satisfaction are unchanged, and nobody has rerun the golden set. What does the lesson say is happening?
options: Nothing actionable, because quality problems should be judged by customer satisfaction rather than by internal edit metrics
A rising edit rate with a flat complaint rate is a system telling you it got worse and nobody outside the team has noticed yet.
The edit rate threshold is set too low, so the fix is to raise it to 30 percent to match the regional baseline
The retrieval index has drifted, so the only reliable response is to rebuild the index from scratch
questions.explanation: The lesson names edit rate as the metric to watch in stages 1 through 3 and the one teams forget to instrument, because it moves within days of a retrieval or prompt regression, well before complaint rates move. The prescribed reading is a quality review of the top ten edits rather than a threshold adjustment, and the same signal measured against the fixed golden set of 40 cases is the comparable weekly number.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
For output this shows up concretely in three places.
The opposite is true: for output this shows up concretely in three places.
questions.explanation: For output this shows up concretely in three places.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what role does KEDA's operator component fill relative to the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler?
options: It replaces the HPA entirely, so the HPA is disabled whenever KEDA manages a workload
It handles scaling between zero and one replica of an idle Deployment, while the HPA manages counts above one and polls the external metrics KEDA exposes
It only scales on CPU and memory, and it never reads event sources like message queues
It rewrites node taints so ordinary agent pods land on GPU nodes
questions.explanation: KEDA works alongside the HPA rather than replacing it. Its operator handles zero-to-one and one-to-zero scaling of an idle Deployment, and above one replica the HPA takes over, reading the external queue metrics that KEDA exposes.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Evaluation: Evals, Golden Datasets, LLM-as-Judge, and When It Lies”, what is the central focus?
options: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust, and the moment a model changes you have no way to know what you traded away.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust, and the moment a model changes you have no way to know what you traded away. This lesson walks the evaluation stack from the bottom up: the golden dataset that anchors everything, the classic metrics that break on open-ended output, the LLM-as-judge technique that replaces them, and the biases that make a judge lie, from position and verbosity preference to rating its own output too high and being misled by a confident wrong answer.

questions.question: Per lesson 70, what is the architectural question that separates a workflow from an agent?
options: How capable the underlying model is, since stronger models enable agents and weaker ones are limited to workflows
Who owns the decision of what happens next: in a workflow your code fixes the path, while in an agent the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use
Whether the system runs on a single server or across a cluster
Whether the prompt uses tools or not, since an agent is simply any system that calls an API
questions.explanation: The lesson says the distinction is not about model capability; both use the same model. It is about who owns the decision of what happens next. A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

questions.question: A team cuts per-call context size by 40% but the change triggers 67% more model calls. Using the lesson's three-lever cost identity, why does this fail to save money?
options: Because the routing classifier always spends more tokens than the context it saved

Because a 40% reduction in context multiplied by a 67% increase in calls reaches roughly break-even under the linear cost model, so the save on lever one is spent back on lever two, the call count, and each added call also retransmits the growing context on every turn
Because reducing context size automatically increases output tokens by the same amount
Because prompt caching is disabled whenever the context changes, wiping out all savings
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Infosys: a 40% reduction in per-call context that triggers 67% more calls reaches break-even under the linear cost model, because 0.60 multiplied by 1.67 is approximately 1.00. The interaction compounds because each added call retransmits accumulated history rather than a fixed-size payload. This is the substitution effect the lesson warns about: naive optimizations shift cost between levers rather than removing it.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Workflow Automation Agents (Browsers, Clicks, and Typing)", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: The model's reasoning rarely fails: grounding fails when the click lands on the wrong element, and blast radius is underestimated when the click submits something real, and both are engineering problems solved before production
Better prompting is the main fix for click accuracy
Screenshots are the only reliable way for an agent to observe a page
Rules-based automation should be replaced entirely by agents
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that both failure modes in this class are engineering problems rather than prompting problems, and that both get solved before the agent ever runs in production.

questions.question: A client submits a task and the peer returns TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED. According to the lesson, what is the correct client behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and open a new task with a fresh messageId
Poll GetTask without limit until the state changes to completed
Treat it as an interrupted state, supply the missing information in another message bound to the same task id, and keep the context
Cancel the task and retry the whole request later with a different payload
questions.explanation: INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED are interrupted states, not terminal ones. The lesson warns that clients handling only completed and failed will strand work that was waiting on one clarification, and that resending as new work loses the task continuity.

questions.question: Why does the Vercel AI SDK earn a place in a serverless lesson rather than an earlier one, per the text?
options: It is the only hosting platform that can run a Lambda function
It replaces the model API entirely, so you no longer call a provider

Streaming is how a disposable, stateless serverless instance can feel like a live conversation, because tokens and tool messages flow back to the client as they are produced even though the instance may vanish as soon as the request ends
It is required before an agent may be deployed at the edge
questions.explanation: The AI SDK's streamText streams tokens and tool-call and tool-result messages back to the client as they are produced, so a serverless instance that is gone the moment the request finishes still delivers a clean, live-feeling response. The toolkit is the bridge between a stateless platform and an interface that appears continuous.

questions.question: A company's support agent reads case history and drafts a refund recommendation for human approval. Following the lesson's three-plane model, which plane decides that the refund draft requires additional checks and must be flagged for human approval?
options: The serving plane, because it selects which model handles the request
The data plane, because it controls which rows the agent can read
The control plane, because it enforces runtime policy and decides whether an action like a refund needs additional checks
The harness, because it owns the agent's memory and context window
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the control plane governs the action. When the agent tries to draft a refund, the control plane applies runtime policy: a refund requires additional checks, so the output is flagged for human approval rather than executed. The serving plane picks the model, the data plane carries the data, and the harness owns the loop.

questions.question: How does the lesson say you should build a progress step list from an agent framework's event stream?
options: Render raw tool arguments and private reasoning as the visible steps
Mark the run done as soon as the last visible token lands
Fake a percentage when the loop has no fixed step count
Use per-item events such as tool_called and tool_output, because a tool call is a unit a human can understand while a token is not
questions.explanation: The lesson points to per-item stream events like tool_called, tool_output, and message_output_created as the level to render a step list from, and warns against showing raw tool JSON or reasoning.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A 2023 paper found LLMs don't robustly use information in the middle of long inputs (the well-documented lost-in-the-middle effect), and Redis's 2026 guidance is blunter: most long-context models show sharp performance drops past ~32K tokens, so benchmark your actual use case rather than trusting the spec sheet.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.

A 2023 paper found LLMs don't robustly use information in the middle of long inputs (the well-documented lost-in-the-middle effect), and Redis's 2026 guidance is not blunter: most long-context models show sharp performance drops past ~32K tokens, so benchmark your actual use case rather than trusting the spec sheet.
questions.explanation: A 2023 paper found LLMs don't robustly use information in the middle of long inputs (the well-documented lost-in-the-middle effect), and Redis's 2026 guidance is blunter: most long-context models show sharp performance drops past ~32K tokens, so benchmark your actual use case rather than trusting the spec sheet.

questions.question: The lesson gives five screens for choosing a workflow and says two of them reject a candidate outright, no matter how well it scores elsewhere. Which two?
options: Volume and variance
A measurable baseline and a named owner
Error asymmetry and volume
Variance and error asymmetry
questions.explanation: The lesson says to reject outright on the measurable baseline and the owner, because without labelled history you cannot score the agent and a workflow with no owner never ships, and it adds that no score rescues either one.

questions.question: Which three question shapes does the lesson say a knowledge graph genuinely beats vector memory on?
options: Relationship-path, multi-hop queries; whole-corpus aggregation questions; and dense, interconnected domains like dependency or citation graphs
Text-similarity lookups; full-text keyword searches; and linguistic paraphrase recall
Standalone fact questions; single-document summaries; and token-length optimization targets
Image retrieval; numeric range filters; and fuzzy date matching across logs
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three shapes where resemblance fails and the graph wins: relationship-path/multi-hop queries, whole-corpus questions like top-themes-in-tickets, and dense, interconnected domains where everything looks similar to everything else.

questions.question: In the lesson's prompt ops layer, why does the team attach the prompt version to every production call and pair traces with evaluations?
options: To prove the prompt passes a spell check before it is published to the library
To increase token usage so cost reporting shows higher utilization
To make it impossible for another team to copy the prompt
So a quality drop becomes attributable: a trace-linked evaluation jumps from a flagged response to the exact prompt version, context, and model parameters that caused it
questions.explanation: The lesson's core prompt-ops habit is pairing trace and evaluation. Aggregate scoring says a problem exists; trace-linked evaluation supplies the why, because a 200-status LLM response can still be wrong, and the trace shows whether the drop correlates with a prompt version, model route, or retrieval source.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: lesson 1 gave you the taxonomy, Lesson 2 the machinery, Lesson 3 the loop.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
Lesson 1 gave you the taxonomy, Lesson 2 the machinery, Lesson 3 the loop.
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 gave you the taxonomy, Lesson 2 the machinery, Lesson 3 the loop.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The opposite is true: it runs BM25, the classic lexical ranking algorithm, alongside vector similarity, and merges the results.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
It runs BM25, the classic lexical ranking algorithm, alongside vector similarity, and merges the results.
questions.explanation: It runs BM25, the classic lexical ranking algorithm, alongside vector similarity, and merges the results.

questions.question: Why does the lesson argue that an agent platform's control plane should be portable and asset-aware rather than tied to a single cloud vendor's native governance?
options: Because native cloud governance is always slower than a custom-built control plane

Because governance expressed in native cloud constructs is non-transferable, so a multi-cloud portfolio needs separate governance stacks in different policy languages, and the tooling that appears free at signup becomes the lock-in mechanism at exit
Because cloud vendors do not offer any governance tooling for AI agents
Because asset-aware governance is required by law in every jurisdiction
questions.explanation: MuleSoft's argument, which the lesson adopts, is that native cloud governance is non-transferable: every policy and audit config is authored in a proprietary schema meaningful only inside that cloud. A multi-cloud portfolio needs separate stacks in different policy languages, and the free-looking tooling becomes lock-in at exit. An asset-aware control plane governs by what the asset is, not by who built it or which cloud it runs on.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Privacy: PII, Data Minimization, Retention, and Consent for AI", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: An agent that touches personal data is allowed to touch the least of it, for the shortest time, on a defensible legal basis, and the person concerned has to be able to tell what was done and stop it
Network security alone is enough to make an agent lawful
Collecting more context is always the way to make an agent smarter
Consent is the only lawful basis under the GDPR
questions.explanation: That is the lesson's central framing: the privacy layer decides which data the security layer even has to defend, and it rests on recognition, minimization, retention, and a real legal basis.

questions.question: For a dense, tabular PDF where every table cell must be reproduced exactly for downstream processing, what does the NVIDIA experiment in lesson 66 show about a general vision-language model versus a specialized extraction pipeline?
options: The general model is faster and more accurate, so it should always be used for tables
The specialized pipeline wins on both accuracy (higher recall@5) and speed, while the general model misread chart elements, missed embedded text, and hallucinated details
Both approaches are equally accurate, so the choice is purely cosmetic
The general model is more accurate but the pipeline is faster, so accuracy should win
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the NVIDIA PDF extraction comparison in which the specialized multistage pipeline beat the 11B vision-language model by 7.2 percent recall@5 and processed pages about 32 times faster, and the error analysis showed the general model misinterpreting elements and hallucinating.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 10 gave you the RAG pattern end to end and ended by promising a deeper look at the retrieval stack: how embedding models differ and how to evaluate retrieval quality.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The opposite is true: lesson 10 gave you the RAG pattern end to end and ended by promising a deeper look at the retrieval stack: how embedding models differ and how to evaluate retrieval quality.
questions.explanation: Lesson 10 gave you the RAG pattern end to end and ended by promising a deeper look at the retrieval stack: how embedding models differ and how to evaluate retrieval quality.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The term for this in the frameworks is an interrupt, and LangGraph exposes it as a function you call inside a graph node: interrupt("Do you approve this action?").
The term for this in the frameworks is not an interrupt, and LangGraph exposes it as a function you call inside a graph node: interrupt("Do you approve this action?").
questions.explanation: The term for this in the frameworks is an interrupt, and LangGraph exposes it as a function you call inside a graph node: interrupt("Do you approve this action?").

questions.question: An invoice page contains hidden text that tells the agent to change a payment beneficiary. Following the lesson, why is the guardrail stack expected to stop this even if the model absorbs the instruction?
options: Because the model reads page content as untrusted and never imports it into its reasoning

Because an allowlist restricts the agent to its one origin and removes the email tool, while a human approval gate stands before the anti-redundant high-value payment action, so the instruction cannot cascade into an action
Because prompt injection can only redirect the agent's answer, never its actions
Because vision model image downscaling drops all hidden text before the model sees it
questions.explanation: In the worked example, the agent reads the injected note but the guardrails hold: the instruction set tells it the user's conversation instructions outrank on-screen content, the allowlist gives it no email tool or other origin to extend to, and the payment is above the approval threshold so the loop pauses for a human who checks the trace. Consequential paths run through controls a person or code owns, so a successful injection does not produce an action.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Agent Loop: Perceive, Reason, Act, Observe, and Where Your Code Lives”, what is the central focus?
options: The one while loop that turns a language model into an agent: the five stages of the loop, the pseudocode that runs underneath every framework, and exactly which parts of it are your code versus the runtime's.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The one while loop that turns a language model into an agent: the five stages of the loop, the pseudocode that runs underneath every framework, and exactly which parts of it are your code versus the runtime's.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Coding Agents (Hermes, Claude Code, and Copilot Under the Hood)", what does a coding agent have that the browser agent from the previous case study did not?
options: A verifier that runs itself, because a test, build, or linter returns a pass or fail the agent can read in the same conversation
A larger model with a longer context window
A human reviewer standing by for every step
A cheaper per-token API contract
questions.explanation: The lesson says the one idea to carry out is that a coding agent gets a verifier that runs itself, which changes both the reliability math and what done means, and contrasts it with the browser agent that needed external verification.

questions.question: In the lesson's worked example, why does the support triage router use a semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 instead of just saving a new file?
options: Semantic versioning makes the file name shorter and easier to type in the terminal
It records the change history and lets the team roll back and identify which version runs in which environment
It is the only format the open-source eval tool accepts for test cases
It forces a full application redeploy on every prompt edit, which is the intended safety mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson says versioning applies code-style tracking to prompts: a history of what changed and why, ability to roll back, and a record of which version runs in which environment. A semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 is that identity. It is about history and environments, not about OS compatibility or the eval tool.

questions.question: Per the lesson “What an Agent Actually Is (LLMs vs Rules vs Workflows)”, what is the central focus?
options: The definitions that matter for the whole track: what separates a rules system, an LLM workflow, and a true agent, plus how to tell which one you're actually building.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The definitions that matter for the whole track: what separates a rules system, an LLM workflow, and a true agent, plus how to tell which one you're actually building.

questions.question: A team wants to move a workload from a managed LLM API to self-hosted GPU infrastructure. Per lesson 73, what is the correct economic decision rule?
options: Self-host whenever the workload is narrow, because narrow tasks always justify fixed hardware
Never self-host, because managed APIs are always cheaper than owning GPUs
Decide on enthusiasm for open-source models rather than measured volume

Model the crossover against metering data and move the workload only when sustained GPU utilization clears roughly 60% to 70%, because below about 30% utilization self-hosting is usually more expensive than the API and the economics only tilt sharply in favor of self-hosting at high utilization
questions.explanation: The lesson applies a utilization threshold: on dedicated GPU inference, below roughly 30% realized utilization self-hosting is frequently more expensive than the API alternative, and above 60% to 70% utilization the economics tilt sharply toward self-hosting. The strategic move is to use telemetry to identify the highest-volume, narrowest tasks and move only those, and to start self-hosting only after metering confirms enough volume and utilization to justify the fixed infrastructure spend.

questions.question: Per the lesson \"Performance: Latency Budgets, Streaming, Batching, and Speculative Execution\", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: Latency is a budget you allocate rather than a wall you hit: you decide the total for each step before shipping, measure TTFT for a human or end-to-end latency for a machine, and spend streaming, batching, and speculative execution on the part that is over target
Latency is one number you push down as far as possible regardless of who is waiting
Time to first token is the only latency metric that matters for every agent
Batching should be the first lever applied to every request, including single interactive ones
questions.explanation: The lesson frames latency as an allocation problem: set the budget from the consumer, measure the number that binds for that consumer, and apply the levers to the step that is over target.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Data Pipelines for RAG: ETL, Connectors, CDC, and Incremental Refresh”, what is the central focus?
options: Connectors (pull versus push), normalizing data before it hits the embedding model, change data capture as the mechanism that turns a polling job into a live one, and incremental refresh that re-embeds only the records that changed.
A history of vector database vendors and their pricing tiers
A review of unrelated content management tools
A summary of corporate governance policies
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Connectors (pull versus push), normalizing data before it hits the embedding model, change data capture as the mechanism that turns a polling job into a live one, and incremental refresh that re-embeds only the records that changed.

questions.question: A computer-use agent keeps misclicking on a dense, JavaScript-heavy portal even though it reads the page structure perfectly. Following the lesson, which improvement is most directly supported?
options: Switch to a hybrid approach that falls back to screenshots when the structured signal runs out, since noisy DOMs are where structured-only agents lose out
Remove the step cap so the agent can keep trying until it succeeds
Widen the origin allowlist to give the agent more page access
Disable the human approval gate so the loop runs faster
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the hybrid approach: default to the cheap structured signal (accessibility tree or DOM) and fall back to screenshots when the structure runs out, because on navigation-heavy, JavaScript-heavy sites where the DOM gets messy, structured-only agents fall behind. A benchmark cited in the lesson showed a vision agent scoring roughly half again better than a text-only tree reader.

questions.question: An Adroit invoice agent must read financial data and apply proprietary anomaly rules. Following the worked example's reasoning, which path does the lesson support and why?
options: An open-source framework like LangGraph, because it runs on your own infrastructure, lets you mix deterministic domain steps with model-driven steps, and keeps the vendor from owning the orchestration of regulated data
A managed platform, because its built-in oracle text is never the bottleneck and it is the fastest route to a demo
Build every wall from primitives, because writing your own router entirely eliminates all retraining and maintenance cost
An open-source framework, because it guarantees you never need to maintain the runtime or implement any orchestration
questions.explanation: Adroit chose an open-source framework because the rules, compliance checks, and approval thresholds are proprietary and auditors need deterministic steps readable in a diff; durable Linux-foundation-governed state and hand-coded domain nodes keep the vendor out of the orchestration of financial data. Building from primitives was rejected because it would mean maintaining a bespoke loop, and the platform was rejected on governance grounds.

questions.question: Per lesson 66, what is the actual mechanism a multimodal agent uses to let the word "the red car" bind to the red pixels in an image?
options: It runs a separate OCR step before the text model sees anything
Cross-attention, where the projected text features selectively focus on relevant parts of the projected image features inside the shared embedding space
It converts the image into a text description first and then embeds that description as normal text
The vision transformer replaces the language model entirely so text and image never need to combine
questions.explanation: The lesson explains fusion as the stage where the model combines projected features into a unified representation, and identifies cross-attention as the mechanism that lets one modality selectively focus on relevant parts of another, which is how a descriptive word binds to the corresponding image content.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Reliability: Retries, Timeouts, and Circuit Breakers for LLM Calls", which of these HTTP status codes should you NOT retry, because retrying it masks a real configuration bug behind delay?
options: 429 (rate limited)
503 (service unavailable)
401 (unauthorized)
504 (gateway timeout)
questions.explanation: The lesson classifies 401 (invalid auth) as a permanent error on your side, along with 400, 403, and 404. Retrying a 401 burns budget and time on a request that will never succeed and hides the real config bug. 429, 503, and 504 are all in the retryable set.

questions.question: In MCP's three roles, what exactly is the client?
options: A separate machine that hosts the model
A component inside the host: each server the host connects to gets its own client object that maintains a dedicated connection and handles protocol messages
The remote program that exposes tools and data
The end user's browser session
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that the client is not a separate machine but a component inside the host, created once per server connection, while the server is the program providing context and capabilities regardless of where it runs.

questions.question: How does the lesson define an integration test for an agent?
options: A test that stubs the model and asserts on a prompt string
A test that runs the whole agent loop against controlled tool side effects, asserting the sequence and outcome, such as the right tool called with the right arguments in the right order
A test that scores real output with an LLM judge against a golden set
A test that measures cost per request under load
questions.explanation: The lesson defines integration tests as running the whole loop with mocked tools that return fixed data, so the assertion is on tool selection, argument formation, ordering, and that nothing destructive happened.

questions.question: The lesson's setup states the goal for the support agent. Which goal does it state?
options: Fully automate every support case so no human is involved
Answer from the model's own knowledge to avoid retrieval cost
Resolve the easy cases end to end and hand the hard ones to a person with full context
Route every case to a human and have the agent draft suggestions only
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the goal is not full automation of everything: the agent resolves the easy cases end to end and escalates the hard ones to a person with full context.

questions.question: Per lesson 69, what is the single most useful reframe of the build-versus-buy decision for agents?
options: Treat it as a choice of where to permanently park your orchestration layer, buying the commodity layers and building the domain logic that is your product
Always build every layer yourself, because any framework or platform is a dependency you cannot audit
Always rent a managed platform, because speed of shipping is the only thing that matters
Choose whichever path shows the lowest initial setup cost, since exit cost is never knowable in advance
questions.explanation: The lesson reframes the question: the build-versus-buy argument is not build the whole stack versus rent the whole stack. It is buy the things that are commodities, build the thing that is your product, and choose your orchestration layer deliberately. Domain logic is the one layer where building is consistently justified, because it is what competitors cannot replicate.

questions.question: A company's agent processes personal data and regulators ask it to demonstrate compliance with data-protection principles. Per lesson 76, what role does the agent audit record play?
options: It is optional decoration that carries no regulatory meaning

GDPR Article 5(2) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance, and the unaltered agent trace is that documentation, built in the record-keeping shape that EU AI Act Article 12 requires for high-risk systems
It is useful only for debugging, never for regulators
It replaces the obligation to comply with the underlying rules themselves
questions.explanation: The lesson frames compliance as the ability to demonstrate. GDPR Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate compliance with, the processing principles, which the ICO frames as keeping evidence of what you did. The EU AI Act's Article 12 requires high-risk systems to allow automatic logging organized around traceability. The unaltered agent trace is the mechanism that makes both demonstrations real.

questions.question: Why does the lesson grow the ticket triager into a ticket resolver?
options: Because routing accuracy is the hardest part of the agent loop
Because the framework cannot produce structured output for a classifier
Because classifying a ticket and stopping leaves the real effort, gathering context, applying policy, and drafting a reply, to a person
Because classification requires a larger model than resolution does
questions.explanation: The lesson says classification alone is not work a human would hand an agent, so the resolver reads the issue, looks up the account and order, checks the refund policy, and drafts a reply a contact center could actually send.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about the harness?
options: The harness is the model itself, and tools are optional extras
The harness is a second model that reviews the first model's edits
The model alone can only emit text; the harness supplies the tools, context management, and execution environment that make it a coding agent
The harness is a fixed program whose behavior cannot be extended
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes the docs describing the harness as the layer providing tools, context management, and execution environment, and adds that tools are what make the model agentic and the tool surface is where capability is extended.
